title: Purpura
subject: Medicine
summary: Purpura are non‑blanching skin hemorrhages >5 mm caused by vascular or platelet dysfunction. Recognising patterns, severity and underlying aetiology guides urgent and long‑term management, especially in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Purpura are palpable or non‑palpable red‑purple lesions ≥5 mm that do not fade with pressure, indicating extravasation of blood into the skin.
b: Measure lesion size: petechiae <5 mm, purpura 5–10 mm, ecchymoses >10 mm.
Differentiate from bruises (history of trauma) and vasculitic lesions (tender, raised).

sections.p: Severity is graded by extent, depth and systemic involvement.
b: Mild: limited to skin, no organ dysfunction.
Moderate: skin plus mild abdominal pain or hematuria.
Severe: skin plus renal failure, CNS bleed, or shock.

sections.p: In East African hospitals the commonest causes are infections, immune‑mediated vasculitis and hematologic disorders.
b: Infection‑related: meningococcemia, severe malaria, dengue, viral hemorrhagic fevers.
IgA vasculitis (Henoch‑Schönlein): palpable purpura on legs/buttocks, abdominal pain, hematuria.
Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis: asthma, eosinophilia, mononeuritis multiplex, purpura.
Thrombotic microangiopathies: TTP, HUS – thrombocytopenia, MAHA, renal failure.
Drug‑induced: penicillins, sulfonamides, herbal remedies.

sections.p: Patients may present with sudden appearance of red‑purple spots, often symmetric on lower limbs, accompanied by systemic clues.
b: Palpable, tender lesions on legs/buttocks.
Abdominal pain, melena, or vomiting (IgA vasculitis).
Neuropathy or asthma symptoms (EGPA).
Fever, malaise, or rapid deterioration (sepsis, TTP).

t.b: Is there thrombocytopenia or anemia? Low platelets suggest TTP/DIC; normal platelets point to vasculitis.
Are schistocytes present? Indicates microangiopathic hemolysis.
Is there hematuria or proteinuria? Suggests renal involvement (IgA vasculitis, HUS).
Is DIC present? Prolonged PT/aPTT, low fibrinogen support sepsis‑related purpura.
Positive MPO‑ANCA supports EGPA; PR3‑ANCA suggests GPA.
Activity <10 % confirms TTP.

b: Rapid fall in platelet count <30 ×10⁹/L.
New neurological deficits or seizures.
Oliguric renal failure or rising creatinine.
Uncontrolled bleeding or shock.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive care.
b: Infection: start empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone + metronidazole) pending cultures.
EGPA: oral prednisolone plus cyclophosphamide for organ‑threatening disease; avoid high‑dose steroids alone if active infection.
TTP: plasma exchange is definitive; if unavailable, give high‑dose methylprednisolone and consider rituximab where feasible.
DIC: treat trigger, give fresh frozen plasma and platelets if bleeding.

sections.p: Monitor organ function and adjust therapy based on response.
b: Weekly platelet count and creatinine until stable.
Educate patients on early signs of bleeding or renal change.
Vaccinate against meningococcus and hepatitis B in at‑risk groups.
Bruising from trauma – usually history of injury, not symmetric, and lesions are not palpable.
Petechial rash of meningococcemia – often accompanied by fever, meningismus, and rapid systemic collapse.
Drug‑induced skin necrosis – tends to be painful, ulcerative, and linked to specific agents.
Normal platelet count does not exclude vasculitis; focus on lesion morphology.
Negative ANCA does not rule out EGPA; eosinophilia and asthma are key.
ADAMTS13 may be normal early in TTP; treat based on clinical pentad.

whenToSeekHelp: New seizures, altered consciousness, or focal neurological signs

faq.q: Can purpura be caused by low platelet count alone?
faq.a: Yes, thrombocytopenia leads to bleeding into the skin, but size and distribution help differentiate from vasculitis.

faq.q: Why is a skin biopsy rarely needed in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: Clinical pattern plus basic labs usually identify the cause; biopsy is reserved for atypical or refractory cases.
Avoid high‑dose steroids if an active bacterial infection is suspected, as they can worsen sepsis.

exam: A 7‑year‑old presents with palpable purpura on the legs, colicky abdominal pain and hematuria – what is the most likely diagnosis and next step? — IgA vasculitis; obtain urinalysis and monitor renal function, give supportive care, steroids only if severe.

A patient with asthma, eosinophilia and new mononeuritis multiplex develops purpuric lesions – which vasculitis is suggested and which drug class is first‑line? — EGPA; oral corticosteroids, add cyclophosphamide for organ involvement.

A febrile adult with meningococcal meningitis develops diffuse purpura and a platelet count of 20 ×10⁹/L – what immediate management is required? — Treat meningococcemia with IV ceftriaxone, give platelet transfusion if bleeding, monitor for DIC.

A 45‑year‑old with fever, confusion, thrombocytopenia, anemia and schistocytes on smear – what condition should you suspect and what is the definitive therapy? — TTP; plasma exchange (or plasma infusion if exchange unavailable).
How does the size of a skin lesion help differentiate petechiae from purpura? — Petechiae are <5 mm, purpura 5–10 mm, ecchymoses >10 mm; size reflects depth of bleeding.
Why might a normal ANCA test not exclude EGPA in a low‑resource hospital? — EGPA can be ANCA‑negative; diagnosis relies on asthma, eosinophilia, neuropathy and purpura.
What red‑flag laboratory finding would prompt urgent referral in a child with purpura? — Platelet count <30 ×10⁹/L or rising creatinine indicating renal involvement.

When is a skin biopsy indicated for purpuric rash in a resource‑limited setting? — Only when the clinical picture is atypical, refractory to treatment, or when vasculitis versus coagulopathy cannot be distinguished.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A systematic history and focused physical exam allow you to differentiate primary vasculitic purpura from infection‑related or coagulopathic causes and to recognise red‑flag organ involvement.
b: Onset: sudden vs. gradual; days to weeks.
Distribution: symmetric lower limbs, trunk, face, mucosa; note any trauma.
Associated symptoms: fever, abdominal pain, melena, arthralgia, hematuria, dyspnoea, asthma exacerbation, neuropathy, seizures.
Medication/ herbal exposure in the past 2 weeks, especially penicillins, sulfonamides, NSAIDs, traditional remedies.
Recent infections: malaria, dengue, meningococcal disease, viral haemorrhagic fevers.
Past medical history: known vasculitis, renal disease, HIV, TB, pregnancy, known hematologic disorder.
Family history of autoimmune disease or hereditary bleeding disorders.

t.b: Tender lesions favour vasculitis; painless lesions favour platelet or coagulation defects. Positive tenderness indicates inflammatory vessel wall involvement.
Look for oral, nasal or conjunctival bleeding. Positive bleeding with normal coagulation points to severe thrombocytopenia.
Detect guarding, palpable mass (possible intussusception) or organomegaly. Positive guarding suggests intra‑abdominal bleed or severe vasculitis.
Assess for focal deficits, seizures, altered mental status. Positive findings indicate CNS involvement, a red‑flag for severe disease (e.g., meningococcemia, TTP).
Identify shock or peripheral vasculitis. Delayed refill suggests hypovolaemia or severe systemic involvement.

t.a: Bedside capillary blood smear (if microscope available)
t.b: Look for schistocytes. Positive schistocytes suggest microangiopathic haemolysis (TTP/HUS). Cannot replace formal peripheral smear analysis.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Prioritise tests that answer the three core questions: (1) Is there thrombocytopenia or coagulopathy? (2) Is there microangiopathic haemolysis? (3) Is there an underlying infection or immune process?
b: Full blood count with peripheral smear – platelet count, haemoglobin, schistocytes.
Prothrombin time/INR and activated partial thromboplastin time – assess coagulation cascade.
Serum fibrinogen – low <1 g/L suggests consumptive coagulopathy (DIC).
D‑dimer – markedly elevated (>2 µg/mL) supports DIC but is non‑specific.
Renal function (creatinine, urea) and urinalysis – hematuria or proteinuria indicates renal vasculitis or TMA.
Liver function tests – assess hepatic involvement in severe sepsis or viral haemorrhagic fever.
Blood cultures and malaria smear – rule out infection‑related purpura.
Serology for dengue, HIV, hepatitis B/C – relevant in low‑resource endemic areas.
ANCA (by immunofluorescence or ELISA) – positive PR3‑ANCA suggests GPA; negative does not exclude EGPA.
IgA level (serum) – may be modestly raised in IgA vasculitis; not diagnostic alone.
ADAMTS13 activity (if available) – <10 % confirms TTP; if unavailable, calculate PLASMIC score.

t.b: Answers whether thrombocytopenia is present. <20 ×10⁹/L is high‑risk for spontaneous bleed; guides urgency of plasma exchange in TTP.
Detects microangiopathic haemolysis. ≥1 % schistocytes supports TTP/HUS; absent schistocytes makes DIC more likely.
Normal PT/aPTT with low platelets points to TTP; prolonged PT/aPTT with low fibrinogen points to DIC.
Low <1 g/L indicates consumptive coagulopathy (DIC). Normal fibrinogen does not exclude TTP.
Very high values (>2 µg/mL) support DIC; modest elevation can be seen in infection or TTP.
Rising creatinine or hematuria indicates renal involvement; guides severity staging for IgA vasculitis or TMA.
Severe deficiency <10 % confirms TTP; if unavailable, use PLASMIC score (≥6 = high probability).
Answers likelihood of severe ADAMTS13 deficiency. Score ≥ 6 → start plasma exchange urgently.
Identify meningococcemia or sepsis; positive culture with purpura mandates antibiotics and DIC management.

t.a: Rapid malaria test or thick smear
t.b: Detects malaria‑related thrombocytopenia; positive result directs antimalarial therapy.

sections.p: Combine clinical pattern, laboratory profile and, when needed, histology to place the patient into a recognised category that drives management urgency.
b: Primary IgA vasculitis (Henoch‑Schönlein): palpable purpura on legs, abdominal pain, arthralgia, IgA deposition; renal involvement = moderate‑severe stage.
Thrombotic microangiopathy (TTP/HUS): severe thrombocytopenia <20 ×10⁹/L, schistocytes, normal coagulation, ADAMTS13 < 10 % (TTP) or typical diarrhoeal prodrome (HUS).
Infection‑related purpura (meningococcemia, severe malaria, dengue): fever, rapid progression, DIC labs (low fibrinogen, high D‑dimer, prolonged PT/aPTT).
Drug‑induced immune thrombocytopenia: abrupt platelet fall after drug exposure, normal coagulation, no schistocytes; improves after drug withdrawal.
Severe vasculitis (ANCA‑associated GPA/EGPA): palpable purpura, systemic organ involvement, positive ANCA (PR3 or MPO).

t.b: Skin‑limited purpura, platelet >50 ×10⁹/L, no organ dysfunction.
Skin plus one organ (e.g., abdominal pain, mild hematuria) without renal failure or CNS bleed.
Skin plus renal failure (creatinine rise >2 mg/dL), CNS involvement, shock, or platelet <20 ×10⁹/L.

sections.p: Several non‑vasculitic entities can mimic purpuric rashes; careful history and targeted tests separate them.

t.b: History of injury, lesions non‑palpable, resolve with colour change; no systemic signs, normal labs.
Prolonged PT/INR, aPTT, normal platelets; purpura often larger ecchymoses; treat with vitamin K or plasma.
Fever, murmur, Janeway lesions; blood cultures positive; may have petechiae but usually associated with cardiac findings.
Palpable purpura after new drug, eosinophilia may be present; ANCA usually negative; improves after drug cessation.
Isolated platelet <30 ×10⁹/L, normal coagulation, no schistocytes; bleeding limited to mucosa and skin; responds to steroids/IVIG.

sections.p: A structured approach ensures rapid control of life‑threatening causes while supporting the patient and preventing organ damage.
b: 1. Immediate stabilization: airway, breathing, circulation; give oxygen, establish IV access, monitor vitals.
2. Urgent laboratory triage: full blood count, peripheral smear, renal function, liver panel, coagulation profile, LDH, haptoglobin, urinalysis, and blood cultures.
3. Identify and treat the underlying cause: start empiric antibiotics for suspected meningococcemia or severe malaria; give high‑dose steroids for immune‑mediated vasculitis if infection excluded.

4. Specific therapy for TTP/HUS: initiate plasma exchange with fresh frozen plasma as soon as TTP is suspected; add caplacizumab where available; avoid platelet transfusion unless life‑threatening bleed.
5. Supportive measures: transfuse red cells for symptomatic anemia, give renal replacement therapy after nephrology review for oliguric renal failure, manage hypertension, and provide analgesia.
6. Monitoring: repeat platelet count, LDH, creatinine, and neurologic exam every 6‑12 h; watch for rising creatinine, falling platelets, or new seizures.
7. Escalation/Referral: call senior clinician or transfer to tertiary centre if platelet <20 ×10⁹/L, uncontrolled bleeding, refractory hypertension, or need for plasma exchange unavailable locally.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Recognising adverse effects and interactions prevents iatrogenic harm, especially where drug monitoring is limited.
b: Corticosteroids – hyperglycaemia, hypertension, infection risk; monitor glucose, treat with insulin if needed, give prophylactic antibiotics only when indicated.
Caplacizumab – bleeding tendency; check for overt bleeding, hold drug if severe hemorrhage, correct coagulopathy before invasive procedures.
Rituximab – infusion reactions, hepatitis B reactivation, TB flare; screen for HBV, HCV, and latent TB before start; give antiviral prophylaxis if HBV positive.
Plasma exchange – volume overload, electrolyte shifts; monitor weight, electrolytes, and give diuretics if pulmonary edema develops.
Antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone for meningococcal disease) – allergic reactions, Clostridioides difficile; review allergy history, use narrow‑spectrum agents when culture results return.

sections.p: Complications may evolve rapidly; clear thresholds trigger higher‑level care.
b: Progressive thrombocytopenia <20 ×10⁹/L with active bleeding – call haematology, arrange plasma exchange or urgent transfer.
Acute kidney injury: creatinine rise >0.3 mg/dL within 48 h or oliguria <0.5 mL/kg/h – involve nephrology, consider dialysis.
Neurologic deterioration: new seizures, altered consciousness, focal deficits – obtain urgent CT, start antiepileptic if seizure persists, refer to neurology.
Severe hypertension >180/110 mmHg with end‑organ signs – start IV antihypertensives, monitor for papilledema, refer to intensive care.
DIC development: platelet <20 ×10⁹/L, fibrinogen <1 g/L, PT/aPTT >1.5 × control – give cryoprecipitate for fibrinogen, consider low‑dose heparin only if thrombotic phenotype dominates.

sections.p: Co‑morbidities and local epidemiology can mask or modify typical findings and affect drug choice.
b: HIV infection – may cause thrombocytopenia, opportunistic infections, and alter steroid safety; screen CD4, avoid high‑dose steroids if CD4 <200 cells/µL without prophylaxis.
Tuberculosis – can present with vasculitic rash; screen with GeneXpert before immunosuppression, give rifampicin‑compatible antiretrovirals if needed.
Malnutrition – reduces plasma protein, affecting drug binding and coagulation tests; correct electrolytes and give vitamin K if prolonged PT.
Pregnancy – alters coagulation (higher fibrinogen) and limits some drugs; use steroids, plasma exchange, and avoid teratogenic agents.
Diabetes – steroids worsen hyperglycaemia; monitor glucose closely and adjust insulin.
Herbal remedies – may contain coumarins or antiplatelet compounds; ask specifically, discontinue before plasma exchange.
Renal or hepatic failure – changes drug clearance; avoid nephrotoxic antibiotics, adjust dosing of steroids based on liver function.
Age extremes – infants have limited blood volume for exchange; elderly have higher bleeding risk and comorbidities; tailor volume and monitoring.

sections.p: Tailoring assessment and therapy to vulnerable populations improves outcomes in low‑resource settings.
b: Children – use weight‑adjusted plasma exchange kits, prioritize oral prednisolone over IV methylprednisolone if IV not available, monitor growth parameters after prolonged steroids.
Pregnant women – prefer plasma exchange over plasma infusion, use prednisolone (inactivated by placenta) for vasculitis, avoid teratogenic immunosuppressants.
Elderly – start plasma exchange slowly to avoid cardiac overload, use lower steroid doses, watch for delirium.
People with HIV – ensure cotrimoxazole prophylaxis continues, treat opportunistic infections before initiating rituximab, monitor for immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome.

Low‑resource hospitals – if plasma exchange unavailable, use high‑dose fresh frozen plasma (15 mL/kg) daily while arranging transfer; use point‑of‑care ultrasound for renal assessment, rely on clinical scoring (PLASMIC) for TTP suspicion.

facts: Purpura size: 5–10 mm; ecchymoses >10 mm; petechiae <5 mm.
Platelet count <20 ×10⁹/L is a red‑flag for life‑threatening purpura.
PLASMIC score ≥6 predicts severe ADAMTS13 deficiency and TTP.
IgA vasculitis (HSP) diagnostic triad: palpable purpura on legs, abdominal pain, hematuria.
TTP classic triad: thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, neurologic change.
DIC D‑dimer markedly elevated; fibrinogen <1 g/L; PT/aPTT prolonged.
First‑line therapy for TTP: daily plasma exchange with fresh frozen plasma.
Rituximab requires screening for HBV, HCV and active TB before use.
In low‑resource settings, skin biopsy is reserved for atypical, non‑diagnostic purpura.

mnemonics.t: Platelet count, Hemolysis, No cancer, No transplant, MCV, INR, Creatinine – predicts severe ADAMTS13 deficiency.

vivas.q: Define purpura and how it differs from petechiae and ecchymoses.
vivas.a: Purpura are non‑blanching red‑purple lesions 5–10 mm; petechiae are <5 mm; ecchymoses are >10 mm.

vivas.q: What bedside test distinguishes a bruise from vasculitic purpura?
vivas.a: Apply gentle pressure with a glass slide; bruises fade (blanch) while vasculitic purpura remain non‑blanching and may be raised.

vivas.q: A child presents with palpable purpura on legs, colicky abdominal pain and hematuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Why can a normal ANCA not exclude EGPA in a low‑resource hospital?
vivas.a: ANCA is positive in only ~40 % of EGPA; clinical features (asthma, eosinophilia, neuropathy) are decisive.

vivas.q: List the three components of the TTP classic triad and why they matter.
vivas.a: Thrombocytopenia (bleeding risk), microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (schistocytes, LDH rise), neurologic change (confusion, seizures); together they prompt urgent plasma exchange.

vivas.q: What laboratory pattern differentiates TTP from DIC?
vivas.a: TTP: normal PT/aPTT, fibrinogen, markedly low platelets, schistocytes; DIC: prolonged PT/aPTT, low fibrinogen, high D‑dimer.

vivas.q: When is a skin biopsy indicated for purpuric rash in a resource‑limited setting?
vivas.a: When the rash is atypical, non‑palpable, or unresponsive to empiric therapy and vasculitis versus infection cannot be distinguished clinically.

vivas.q: What is the first‑line treatment for TTP and a key contraindication?
vivas.a: Daily plasma exchange with fresh frozen plasma; platelet transfusion is contraindicated unless life‑threatening bleeding.

vivas.q: Explain why high‑dose steroids should be used cautiously in HIV patients with CD4 <200 cells/µL.
vivas.a: Steroids can worsen opportunistic infections; benefits must be weighed against risk and prophylaxis considered.

vivas.q: What are the key history questions for a patient with new purpura?
vivas.a: Onset, progression, trauma, recent infections, drug/herbal exposure, fever, abdominal pain, urinary symptoms, asthma, neuropathy, travel, HIV/TB status.

vivas.q: Describe the step‑by‑step examination of purpuric lesions.
vivas.a: Inspect distribution, measure size, assess blanchability, palpate for tenderness or raised lesions, look for edema, check mucosa, assess for joint swelling, note any neurologic deficits.

vivas.q: What is the PLASMIC score and its threshold for high risk?
vivas.a: Score 0–7; ≥6 predicts severe ADAMTS13 deficiency and warrants immediate plasma exchange.

vivas.q: Why is dialysis initiation not a student‑level decision in TTP?
vivas.a: Dialysis requires nephrology assessment; students should arrange urgent referral when oliguria or rising creatinine occurs.

vivas.q: How does IgA vasculitis cause intussusception?
vivas.a: IgA deposition in intestinal vessels leads to submucosal edema and hemorrhage, creating a lead point that telescopes the bowel.

vivas.q: What is the immunological basis of severe post‑transfusion purpura?
vivas.a: Recipient forms anti‑HPA‑1a antibodies after exposure to donor platelets; these antibodies destroy both transfused and autologous platelets.

vivas.q: What is the fundamental pathogenetic driver of ANCA‑associated vasculitis with PR3 antibodies?
vivas.a: Auto‑antibodies activate neutrophils causing necrotizing small‑vessel inflammation.

vivas.q: When should rituximab be added to TTP therapy?
vivas.a: In refractory or relapsing TTP, or when ADAMTS13 activity remains <10 % after plasma exchange.

vivas.q: What are the red‑flag signs that mandate urgent referral in a child with purpura?
vivas.a: Platelets <20 ×10⁹/L, rapid rise in creatinine, new neurologic deficits, persistent fever, or signs of shock.

mcqs.q: A 45‑year‑old woman with asthma, eosinophilia and new mononeuritis multiplex develops purpuric lesions. Which test is least likely to confirm the diagnosis?
mcqs.e: Elevated IgE is nonspecific; ANCA, imaging and biopsy are more diagnostic for EGPA.

mcqs.q: A febrile adult with meningococcal meningitis develops diffuse purpura and platelet count 18 ×10⁹/L. Which condition best explains this picture?
mcqs.e: Meningococcal sepsis commonly precipitates DIC with severe thrombocytopenia and purpura.

mcqs.q: A 50‑year‑old man has fever, confusion, platelet 15 ×10⁹/L, hemoglobin 8 g/dL, schistocytes and normal PT/aPTT. What is the priority treatment?
mcqs.e: Findings are classic for TTP; plasma exchange is the urgent life‑saving therapy.

mcqs.q: Which size cut‑off distinguishes petechiae from purpura?
mcqs.e: Petechiae are lesions smaller than 5 mm; purpura are 5–10 mm.

mcqs.q: In a low‑resource hospital, which investigation is most helpful to confirm IgA vasculitis?
mcqs.e: IgA vasculitis is usually diagnosed clinically; biopsy is rarely available.

mcqs.q: Which medication is contraindicated in active TTP unless life‑threatening bleeding occurs?
mcqs.e: Platelet transfusion can worsen microthrombi formation in TTP.

mcqs.q: A child with HSP develops sudden abdominal pain and a palpable mass. What is the most likely complication?
mcqs.e: IgA deposition causes bowel edema, creating a lead point for intussusception.

cases.v: A 6‑year‑old girl is brought to the clinic with a 2‑day history of non‑blanching purple spots on both ankles and buttocks. She has mild colicky abdominal pain and a single episode of gross hematuria. No fever, no recent drug exposure. Platelet count 210 ×10⁹/L, creatinine 0.7 mg/dL, urinalysis shows 2+ blood, no protein.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?

qs.a: Supportive care; monitor urine output and blood pressure; consider short course of oral steroids if abdominal pain worsens or renal involvement progresses.

qs.q: Which red‑flag would prompt urgent referral?
qs.a: Rapid rise in creatinine, platelet count <20 ×10⁹/L, new neurologic signs, or uncontrolled gastrointestinal bleeding.

cases.v: A 48‑year‑old man presents with fever, confusion, and diffuse petechial rash. Labs: platelets 12 ×10⁹/L, hemoglobin 9 g/dL, LDH 800 U/L, peripheral smear shows schistocytes, PT 13 s, aPTT 32 s, fibrinogen 1.2 g/L. No obvious source of infection.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
What is the first‑line definitive therapy?
qs.a: Urgent daily plasma exchange with fresh frozen plasma, plus corticosteroids.

qs.q: If plasma exchange is unavailable, what is the best alternative?
qs.a: High‑dose plasma‑rich fresh frozen plasma administered rapidly, while arranging transfer to a center with exchange capability.

mistakes: Confusing the classic TTP pentad with diagnostic criteria; rely on ADAMTS13 or PLASMIC score.
Using platelet transfusion routinely in TTP; it is contraindicated unless massive bleeding.
Ordering cryoprecipitate for TTP; it has no role and may worsen volume overload.
Assuming normal ANCA excludes EGPA; remember ANCA sensitivity is low.
Initiating dialysis without nephrology input; always refer first.
Neglecting HCV and TB screening before rituximab in endemic areas.
Treating all purpura with antibiotics; differentiate infection‑related from vasculitic causes.
Memorising size cut‑offs incorrectly; petechiae are <5 mm, purpura 5–10 mm, ecchymoses >10 mm.
